articles.title: Decoração de Natal em SP vira alvo de críticas nas redes sociais; prefeitura explica contratos e gastos de R$ 19,7 milhões | G1
articles.standfirst: Enfeites instalados em postes da Avenida Paulista e do Centro foram comparados a desenhos infantis feitos em papelão; prefeitura afirma que estruturas são de outro contrato, ligado à concessão de iluminação pública, mas não explicou o que exatamente está previsto no documento que gerou críticas.
articles.summary: Enfeites instalados em postes da Avenida Paulista e do Centro foram comparados a desenhos infantis feitos em papelão; prefeitura afirma que estruturas são de outro contrato, ligado à concessão de iluminação pública, mas não explicou o que exatamente está previsto no documento que gerou críticas.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

A decoração de Natal instalada nesta semana na Avenida Paulista e em regiões do Centro de São Paulo virou alvo de críticas nas redes sociais. Imagens de Papai Noel, anjinhos, velas, sinos e guirlandas colocadas em postes foram questionadas por usuários pela aparência dos enfeites. Alguns deles foram comparados a desenhos infantis feitos em papelão.

O g1 procurou a Prefeitura de São Paulo para entender quanto custa a decoração natalina deste ano e quais contratos são responsáveis pelas estruturas instaladas na cidade. A administração municipal tem pelo menos duas contratações relacionadas aos festejos, que somam R$ 19,7 milhões.

Um dos projetos é o "Natal Iluminado Paulista 2026", sob responsabilidade do Instituto Girassol, com previsão de investimento de R$ 6,1 milhões . O segundo é o "Natal no Centro Histórico de São Paulo", realizado por meio da Secretaria Municipal de Turismo, com orçamento de R$ 13,6 milhões . O plano de trabalho deste último projeto foi apresentado pelo Instituto Agon.

Segundo a prefeitura, os painéis com imagens natalinas instalados nos postes da Avenida Paulista e do entorno não estão incluídos no projeto do Instituto Girassol nem no do Instituto Agon. Eles foram custeados por meio do contrato de concessão de iluminação pública da cidade , que prevê a realização de projetos especiais de iluminação.

A decoração de Natal instalada nesta semana na Avenida Paulista e em regiões do Centro de São Paulo virou alvo de críticas nas redes sociais. — Foto: Reprodução

Os questionamentos também chegaram ao Ministério Público de São Paulo (MP-SP). O deputado estadual Toninho Vespoli (PSOL) protocolou uma representação no órgão pedindo explicações sobre os gastos públicos com a decoração natalina (leia mais abaixo).

Em nota, a Prefeitura de São Paulo afirmou que os enfeites estão sendo instalados por meio da concessão de iluminação pública da cidade, cujo contrato prevê a execução de projetos especiais de iluminação.

A gestão do prefeito Ricardo Nunes (MDB), porém, não explicou o que exatamente está previsto no contrato em relação a esses projetos ou porque uma empresa de iluminação pública instalou enfeites natalinos na cidade.

O projeto "Natal Iluminado Paulista 2026", de R$ 6,1 milhões, prevê intervenções na Avenida Paulista e no Parque Prefeito Mário Covas, na Bela Vista, além de aproximadamente 100 atividades gratuitas, como oficinas, contação de histórias, shows, corais, cortejos e apresentações de música, dança e teatro.

O Instituto Girassol, responsável pelo projeto, informou que a decoração sob sua responsabilidade inclui uma passarela cenográfica elevada, um túnel de luz com previsão de 200 arcos ao longo de aproximadamente dois quilômetros da ciclovia, 200 elementos luminosos de LED e 15 cenários interativos.

No Parque Prefeito Mário Covas, estão previstas estruturas como pórtico de entrada, Casa do Noel, palco acessível, árvore cenográfica e espaço coberto para oficinas.

Segundo o instituto, a montagem e a operação mobilizam mais de 260 profissionais, sem contar artistas e equipes da programação cultural. O plano prevê aproximadamente R$ 2 milhões para contratações artísticas.

A abertura ao público está prevista para esta sexta-feira (27), com programação até 17 de janeiro de 2027.

Sede da Prefeitura de São Paulo em imagem de divulgação do Projeto Natal Iluminado. — Foto: Divulgação

Já o projeto "Natal no Centro Histórico" tem orçamento de R$ 13.615.683,71, conforme o plano de trabalho do Instituto Agon apresentado à Secretaria Municipal de Turismo.

A proposta prevê decoração, iluminação especial, cenografia e atrações gratuitas em 11 pontos da região central, entre eles a sede da prefeitura, no Edifício Matarazzo, o Viaduto do Chá, a Praça do Patriarca, a Praça dos Correios, o Viaduto Santa Ifigênia, o Mosteiro de São Bento, a Praça da Sé e o Theatro Municipal.

Entre as estruturas previstas estão uma árvore cenográfica de 23 metros de altura em frente à sede da Prefeitura, uma pista de gelo na Praça do Patriarca, um túnel iluminado de 200 metros no Viaduto Santa Ifigênia, roda-gigante e carrossel na Praça da Sé, além de arcos luminosos em ruas do Centro.

O documento estima atender 2 milhões de pessoas durante o período de execução, previsto entre 26 de novembro de 2026 e 5 de janeiro de 2027.

Do total de R$ 13,6 milhões, R$ 12,8 milhões estão previstos para serviços diretamente relacionados à execução do projeto. Outros R$ 700,1 mil são destinados à divulgação, e R$ 96,9 mil, a despesas administrativas indiretas.

O plano também prevê gastos com segurança, brigadistas, limpeza, sanitários químicos, acessibilidade, equipes técnicas e divulgação. Entre os itens estão R$ 249,2 mil para brigadistas e primeiros socorros e R$ 259,1 mil para vigilância patrimonial noturna.

A polêmica também chegou ao Ministério Público de São Paulo (MP-SP). O deputado estadual Toninho Vespoli (PSOL) protocolou uma representação no órgão pedindo explicações sobre os gastos públicos com a decoração natalina.

O parlamentar questionou os valores envolvidos diante da aparência dos enfeites que passaram a circular nas redes sociais.

Até a última atualização desta reportagem, o Ministério Público não havia respondido sobre o recebimento da representação ou sobre eventuais providências relacionadas ao caso.

articles.title: Vice-presidente das Filipinas, Sara Duterte diz que sua renúncia está 'fora de questão' em meio ao processo de impeachment | G1
articles.standfirst: Sara Duterte é alvo de um processo de impeachment devido a um suposto acúmulo de riqueza inexplicável. Seu pai, Rodrigo Duterte, ex-presidente do país, está preso em Haia, aguardando ser julgado na próxima semana por crimes contra a humanidade.
articles.summary: Sara Duterte é alvo de um processo de impeachment devido a um suposto acúmulo de riqueza inexplicável. Seu pai, Rodrigo Duterte, ex-presidente do país, está preso em Haia, aguardando ser julgado na próxima semana por crimes contra a humanidade.
articles.body:
Vice-presidente das Filipinas, Sara Duterte (à esquerda), e presidente do país, Ferdinand Marcos Jr. — Foto: AP

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

A vice-presidente das Filipinas , Sara Duterte, afirmou na sexta-feira (27) que sua renúncia está fora de questão, apesar do processo de impeachment em andamento sobre seu suposto acúmulo de riqueza inexplicável.

Duterte, filha do ex-presidente Rodrigo Duterte , tem sido a favorita nas pesquisas de opinião para se tornar a próxima presidente em 2028.

"Renunciar está fora de questão", disse ela a repórteres em um encontro de fim de ano com a imprensa.

"É algo que não posso fazer porque sinto que seria uma traição aos 32,2 milhões de pessoas que votaram em mim e, claro, ao público em geral, se eu renunciasse."

Os procuradores filipinos concentraram o processo de impeachment contra Duterte em uma única acusação de enriquecimento ilícito, abandonando outras três acusações, na tentativa de concluir o julgamento até o final deste ano, antes que a atenção se volte para as eleições de 2028.

Duterte nega qualquer irregularidade e classificou o processo como assédio político.

Uma condenação a destituiria do cargo e a desqualificaria para cargos políticos para sempre, pondo fim às suas ambições presidenciais.

Em seu julgamento de impeachment, Duterte disse que estava se preparando para o pior e alertou que um veredicto de culpada traria "muitas consequências", incluindo a perda de empregos em seus gabinetes.

O impeachment dela foi a maior escalada em um conflito político entre Duterte e o presidente Ferdinand Marcos Jr., que eram aliados poderosos quando concorreram juntos e venceram as eleições de 2022, antes de sua relação azedar.

Marcos, que está limitado a um único mandato e não pode se candidatar em 2028, afirmou que o impeachment é uma questão legislativa.

Em um processo criminal separado , Duterte também é acusada de três crimes de ameaças graves relacionados a comentários que fez sobre o presidente Ferdinand Marcos Jr., a primeira-dama e um ex-presidente da Câmara dos Deputados. Ela nega as acusações .

Ela também disse que esperava que seu pai, Rodrigo Duterte, que foi presidente de 2016 a 2022, não tivesse um julgamento justo quando fosse a julgamento no Tribunal Penal Internacional em Haia, na segunda-feira (30).

Ele é acusado de crimes contra a humanidade durante sua "guerra contra as drogas" de seis anos, período no qual milhares de pessoas foram mortas, muitas em circunstâncias misteriosas.

"Este é o único caso restante apenas no TPI, e eu acho que o TPI, após a união das superpotências, gostaria de deixar claro que está certo", disse ela.

Ela disse que não era justo que seu pai fosse obrigado a comparecer ao tribunal todos os dias para as audiências.

"Não acho que ele consiga se concentrar e dedicar o tempo e a atenção necessários", disse ela. "É injusto exigir isso de um homem de 81 anos."

Duterte, de 81 anos, está preso em Haia, na Holanda, desde março de 2025 e enfrenta acusações de homicídio. Promotores disseram que Duterte criou, financiou e armou esquadrões da morte para identificar e matar supostos traficantes e usuários de drogas enquanto esteve no poder entre 2016 e 2022. Leia mais abaixo.

Duterte sempre afirmou que instruiu a polícia a matar apenas em legítima defesa e tem defendido consistentemente a repressão.

Juízes de apelação do tribunal rejeitaram um pedido para anular o julgamento de Duterte e afirmaram que a corte tem jurisdição sobre o caso.

Em casos anteriores, o TPI levou até um ano entre a confirmação das acusações e o início do julgamento.

Assassinatos em áreas pobres das Filipinas

Presidente das Filipinas, Rodrigo Duterte, conversa com jornalistas na segunda-feira (30) — Foto: King Rodriguez/ Malacanang Presidential Photographers Division/ AP

Segundo a polícia, 6.200 pessoas foram mortas durante operações antidrogas que teriam terminado em tiroteios durante o governo Duterte.

No entanto, ativistas dizem que o verdadeiro número de mortos foi muito maior, incluindo milhares de usuários de drogas em comunidades carentes — muitos deles marcados em "listas de observação" locais e mortos em circunstâncias misteriosas.

O TPI afirma que até 30.000 pessoas podem ter sido assassinadas pela polícia ou por indivíduos não identificados.

A polícia nega as acusações de execuções sistemáticas e acobertamentos feitas por grupos de direitos humanos.

A prisão de Duterte ocorreu após anos de provocações ao TPI, desde que ele retirou unilateralmente as Filipinas do tratado fundador do tribunal em 2019. A Corte investiga supostos crimes contra a humanidade e alega ter jurisdição sobre crimes ocorridos enquanto o país ainda era membro.

O governo filipino se recusava a cooperar, mas a atual administração mudou de postura em novembro de 2024, sinalizando que cumpriria um eventual mandado de prisão.

articles.title: Suspeito de matar pastor conhecia dinâmica das orações, diz mulher | G1
articles.standfirst: Ao g1, Alessandra Lopes relatou que Bruno Marcelo Vaz da Silva era assíduo nas orações. José Bezerra, de 61 anos, foi morto a facadas em Cidade Ocidental.
articles.summary: Ao g1, Alessandra Lopes relatou que Bruno Marcelo Vaz da Silva era assíduo nas orações. José Bezerra, de 61 anos, foi morto a facadas em Cidade Ocidental.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

O suspeito de matar a facadas o pastor José Bezerra, de 61 anos , dentro de uma igreja em Cidade Ocidental , no Entorno do Distrito Federal, conhecia a dinâmica das orações da congregação. A informação foi relatada ao g1 pela frequentadora Alessandra Lopes, que afirmou que Bruno Marcelo Vaz da Silva participava de forma assídua das orações.

O crime aconteceu na quarta-feira (25), e Bruno foi preso no mesmo dia. Ele deve passar por audiência de custódia nesta sexta-feira (27). Em nota ao g1 , a defesa de Bruno Marcelo informou que acompanha o caso e adotará as medidas cabíveis, e disse ainda que o procedimentos se encontra em fase inicial, sem decisão definitiva sobre a responsabilidade penal do acusado (leia nota completa abaixo) .

Segundo a investigação, José Bezerra ministrava um culto na igreja quando foi atacado pelas costas a golpes de faca. O crime ocorreu durante um momento de oração.

'Conhecia perfeitamente a dinâmica das orações': diz mulher que frequenta igreja sobre suspeito de matar pastor a facadas durante culto — Foto: Reprodução/TV Anhanguera

De acordo com o delegado Aluísio Nascimento, o suspeito tinha o desejo de se tornar pastor e frequentou o templo por cerca de um ano e meio. Em uma foto publicada nas redes sociais, é possível ver Bruno Marcelo Vaz da Silva de joelhos enquanto recebia a bênção.

Após não conseguir ser consagrado como pastor, o suspeito se afastou da congregação. "O autor decidiu parar de frequentar a igreja por volta de março e, depois, comparecia apenas esporadicamente, até o dia em que cometeu o crime" , afirmou o delegado.

O pastor morava em Cidade Ocidental há quase 40 anos, onde vivia com a esposa e teve dois filhos e uma filha, sendo natural do Ceará. José já havia sido garçom antes de se aposentar e decidiu se dedicar integralmente à igreja. Pastor há 20 anos, ele foi fundador da Igreja Evangélica Pentecostal Luz e Vida, onde o crime aconteceu.

A Prefeitura de Cidade Ocidental publicou uma nota de pesar sobre a morte do pastor, e manifestou condolências aos familiares, amigos e à comunidade evangélica.

A defesa de Bruno Marcelo Vaz da Silva informa que acompanha o caso e adotará as medidas jurídicas cabíveis no interesse de seu constituinte. O procedimento ainda se encontra em fase inicial, sem decisão definitiva sobre a responsabilidade penal do acusado. Por essa razão, a defesa não comentará aspectos específicos do caso nem antecipará argumentos que serão apresentados oportunamente nos autos.

A defesa confia na atuação das instituições competentes e espera que a apuração observe o devido processo legal, o contraditório, a ampla defesa e a presunção de inocência. Novas informações serão divulgadas exclusivamente pelos canais oficiais da defesa, quando oportuno e sem prejuízo da investigação ou da intimidade das pessoas envolvidas.

articles.title: From counting to 100,000 to building a $5 billion empire: MrBeast's extraordinary business journey
articles.summary: Jimmy Donaldson has turned a childhood obsession with YouTube into a business empire valued at more than $5 billion.
articles.body: Jimmy Donaldson has turned a childhood obsession with YouTube into a business empire valued at more than $5 billion. Better known as MrBeast, the 28-year-old creator has built a global audience through outrageous challenges, huge giveaways and ambitious productions. But his next challenge may have little to do with breaking subscriber records. As Beast Industries expands into entertainment, food, technology and financial services, Donaldson is trying to prove that his company can thrive without depending entirely on his face and name.MrBeast's $5 billion empire is growing beyond YouTubeDonaldson's journey began in Greenville, North Carolina, where he started uploading videos as MrBeast6000. His early content included gaming streams and commentary about other creators. That changed in 2017, when a video of him counting from zero to 100,000 went viral. The unusual challenge took more than 40 hours and helped him cross the one-million-subscriber mark.Today, his main YouTube channel has more than 500 million subscribers. Yet the real story is how he turned that audience into a commercial operation.Beast Industries has grown into a company with nearly 800 employees. Investors have valued the business at more than $5 billion, while its 2024 revenue reportedly reached $473 million. The company also expected revenue to nearly double in 2025, according to a pitch deck obtained by Business Insider.Its portfolio now includes Feastables, Lunchly, MrBeast Lab and Viewstats. Donaldson has also moved into streaming with Amazon's Beast Games, backed by a reported $100 million deal. Despite its huge audience, the first season reportedly cost him tens of millions of dollars.The expansion has also brought new ambitions. Beast Industries has explored mobile services, financial products through its acquisition of Step and a marketplace for online creators. These plans suggest Donaldson wants to build a company with a life beyond viral videos.MrBeast wants Beast Industries to succeed without himOne of Donaldson's biggest business challenges is reducing the company's dependence on its founder. He appointed former Shutterfly CEO Jeffrey Housenbold to lead Beast Industries and has brought in experienced executives to manage its growing operations.The strategy makes sense. A company worth billions needs more than one popular personality to sustain its growth. Donaldson has also explored new content formats, including an animated series and a novel written with James Patterson.However, his public image remains closely tied to giving. Through Beast Philanthropy, he has turned online attention into campaigns supporting people in need. His earlier projects included Team Trees, which aimed to plant 20 million trees.That charitable identity has also shaped how he talks about wealth. In a 2022 post, Donaldson wrote: "No matter how big I get I'll never own a mansion, yacht, Lamborghini etc," he tweeted in 2022. "All I want is to make the best videos possible and help as many people as I can while doing it."His business has not been without problems. The MrBeast Burger partnership led to lawsuits, while Beast Games faced allegations from contestants about working conditions and safety. Beast Industries has also faced an employment lawsuit, which the company has broadly denied.For Donaldson, the next chapter is about more than creating another record-breaking video. articles.title: The young hikers finding friendship and fresh air offline
articles.summary: From hiking in the Peak District hills to the city parks of Leicester - we talk to several young people who've embraced walking groups and feel better for it.
articles.body:
After years toiling all day at a desk as an aerospace engineer in Istanbul, 26-year-old Mohannad Najjar decided to swap his screen for a degree in nature and theology in Cambridge and a volunteering gig as a scout leader.

He walks in the countryside every weekend and has hiked in wild locations in the Scottish Highlands, which he credits with helping him think clearly.

"I just want to see something that's untouched, to be in nature," he says. "When you come in from a hike or a walk, you just feel different."

Najjar is one of a growing number of young hikers in the UK. Nearly 9% of 16-34 year-olds are regular hill walkers or hikers, according to Sport England, up from 2.3% eight years ago.

Many young walkers' groups from Inverness to Nottinghamshire have seen their membership rise over the past two years, according to the Ramblers walking charity.

Demand has nearly doubled for a course it offers teaching map and compass skills to 18-25 year-olds.

Many who sign up want to ditch their phones and no longer rely on a blue dot to navigate, says Alistair Cooper, who leads the Out There Award programme.

"There's a cohort that missed out on outdoorsy, fun stuff during Covid. They want to get out and explore - but often don't know where to start."

Some 83% of people in the UK live in towns and cities, according to the UN, where research suggests noise, traffic, stress and information overload put huge demands on our brains, affecting our mental health.

"Nature is the environment we are adapted to, and being close to it brings benefits such as improved wellbeing, brain function and physical performance," says Dr Danny Longman, lecturer in human evolutionary physiology from Loughborough University.

"There is a theory that simply paying attention to trees and leaves allows our brains to recover," he says.

Environmental science student Deborah Odutayo, 24, described going through "an identity crisis".

"I didn't see myself as someone who works behind a desk from 9 to 5," she said.

After solo travelling, Odutayo had dreams of living abroad but didn't know how to finance them. So she decided to change her mindset.

"I just need to be outside, essentially. That's how I started like doing solo hikes and stuff. It feels very therapeutic - mostly for my mental health."

She's since hiked in Kent and the Peak District, among other locations, and camped with an outdoor group in Dorset.

Learning how to get around without using her phone or digital maps is something she is proud of, saying it feels "more intentional and grounding".

Walking gives people "an instant friend group" when life is in flux, says Miranda Chambers-Reid, who leads a Ramblers' walking group for people in their 20s and 30s in Sheffield.

"They don't want all of their friends to be work friends or old uni friends," she says.

As a mum of a seven-year-old, she made a similar decision when she joined: "I thought, I don't want all of my friends to be mum friends."

Over the last two years, the group has increased from 250 members to 350.

For some it's more about a sense of achievement says Chambers-Reid, who herself covers about 30 miles of walking a week.

"I work in an office and I can't see the sky so whenever possible I will be outside."

For Sej Chauhan, 27, her walking group is about making connections while keeping costs down.

"There's a growing interest in socialising in ways that don't involve drinking alcohol or spending lots of money," she says.

Chauhan set up Girls Who Walk in her home town of Leicester after a lonely year spent studying in Bristol.

To make that experience easier for others, the group's focus is on walking in parks, talking and female companionship. And there's always a stop for coffee.

In two years, the group has grown to more than 300 members - most are 25-35 years old.

"There's no pressure, no barriers with walking," Chauhan says. "Social media can often fill the void outside of work and home, but it doesn't provide the connection that people are craving."

Not everyone can access green space easily or has the time to go hiking because of work or childcare commitments.

Here are Longman's tips for getting your nature fix as close as possible to home:

Move in nature - an urban park or garden will do

Listen to the sounds of the elements, like wind, rain, birdsong

Smell the distinctive scent of pine forests, breathe in the outdoors

If you are indoors, bring the sounds and imagery of nature into your home using apps

articles.title: A New York mother transferred four plots of land to her daughter during financial trouble in 2012, then sought three of them back when her daughter planned to sell; an appeals court upheld the daughter's ownership
articles.summary: A New York mother who transferred four plots of land to her daughter during a period of financial difficulty went to court more than a decade later to
articles.body: A New York mother who transferred four plots of land to her daughter during a period of financial difficulty went to court more than a decade later to reclaim three of them. The dispute began after her daughter announced plans to sell the properties in 2024. However, on November 25, 2026, the New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Third Department, upheld the daughter's ownership, finding that the mother had failed to establish a legal basis for recovering the land.In its published decision in Chernow v. Maerling, 2026 NY Slip Op 07031, published by the New York State Law Reporting Bureau and available on Justia, the appeals court examined whether the 2012 transfer was an outright gift or an arrangement under which the daughter was expected to return the properties. It concluded that the evidence supported the finding that the transfer was a gift and that there was no promise to give the land back.Mother transferred four properties during financial troubleAccording to the court's November 25 decision, Lynn B Chernow transferred four parcels of land in Sullivan County to her daughter, Melissa Maerling, through a deed executed in September 2012. At the time, Chernow was experiencing serious financial difficulties. She and her then-husband had been advised by an attorney to transfer the properties to protect them from debt collection efforts.During the trial, Maerling's father testified that the transfer was intended to ensure their daughter could retain the properties for her future. He described it as a gift rather than a temporary arrangement. Maerling also understood the transfer as an early inheritance. Although Chernow continued maintaining the properties, paying some taxes and collecting rental income, the daughter maintained that these activities did not mean her mother had retained ownership. Chernow also continued operating a business on one of the properties without paying rent.Dispute began when daughter planned to sellThe disagreement emerged in January 2024, when Maerling informed her mother that she intended to sell the properties. Chernow objected and filed a lawsuit in March 2024, seeking a constructive trust over three of the four parcels her daughter still owned. A constructive trust is an equitable legal remedy that allows a court to recognise a beneficial ownership interest when retaining legal title would be unjust.Chernow argued that the properties had been transferred under an understanding that they would eventually be returned to her. However, Maerling disputed this account, maintaining that the transfer was an outright gift and that she had never promised to return the land. Following a nonjury trial, the Sullivan County Supreme Court dismissed the mother's complaint. It found that she had failed to establish the necessary elements of a constructive trust and that her claim was also barred by laches, a legal doctrine concerning unreasonable delay in pursuing a claim. Chernow appealed the judgment.Appeals court finds no promise to return propertiesThe Appellate Division agreed with the lower court that the transfer was an outright gift. It noted that the deed conveyed the properties to Maerling without reserving any ownership rights for her mother. Under New York law, establishing a constructive trust generally requires four elements: a confidential relationship, a promise, a transfer made in reliance on that promise and unjust enrichment.The court found that Chernow had not established these requirements. In particular, there was no evidence that Maerling had expressly or implicitly promised to return the properties. The mother also failed to demonstrate that she transferred the land in reliance on such a promise. The judges considered Chernow's continued involvement in maintaining the properties and collecting rental income. However, they found that these activities were consistent with caretaking arrangements and did not establish that she had retained ownership.Court disagrees with lower court on delayAlthough the appeals court upheld the dismissal, it disagreed with the lower court's finding that the mother's claim was barred by laches. It explained that Maerling had not acted in a way that contradicted her mother's alleged understanding for most of the period following the transfer. The dispute arose when the daughter announced her intention to sell the properties in January 2024.Chernow objected promptly and filed her lawsuit two months later. The appeals court therefore found that her delay did not justify barring the claim under laches. It also rejected the conclusion that the lawsuit was time-barred. The six-year limitation period began when Maerling repudiated the alleged promise to return the properties, which occurred in January 2024. The March 2024 lawsuit was therefore filed within the applicable period.Daughter retains ownershipOn November 25, 2026, the Appellate Division affirmed the judgment dismissing Chernow's complaint and awarded costs to Maerling.The decision means the daughter retains ownership of the three disputed parcels. Although the appeals court rejected the lower court's reasoning on laches and the statute of limitations, it upheld the outcome because the mother had failed to establish the requirements for a constructive trust.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'I did a great thing': Trump backs Jensen Huang's 'second term' at Nvidia
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has defended his intervention in Nvidia's leadership row, saying the return of chief executive Jensen Huang was a \"great thing\"
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has defended his intervention in Nvidia's leadership row, saying the return of chief executive Jensen Huang was a "great thing" for the US and the world. Trump praised Huang's contribution to the chipmaker, saying he was an important part of the company and predicting that he would perform even better in his second stint, despite concerns raised by US intelligence officials over possible national security risks linked to his personal associations.Speaking during a Thanksgiving call with US military personnel alongside First Lady Melania Trump from his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida on Thursday (local time), Trump said Huang was happy to return to Nvidia and had described the development as his "second term".Asked whether he had spoken to Huang since his return to the company's leadership, Trump said, "No. But I probably will sometime prior to his... I guess he's starting essentially on Monday. I think he's a very important part of NVIDIA."Praising Huang's role in Nvidia's chip development, Trump referred to the company's Blackwell processors and said newer products were expected to outperform them."He's got, outside of Blackwell, the chip Blackwell, that's the hot one right now. But that will be obsolete in a year. He's got two new ones coming out that are blowing Blackwell away. Without him, I just don't know. You know, everybody's replaceable, I guess."Trump said he had been concerned about Nvidia's performance and stock movements before Huang's return, adding that the chief executive was pleased to resume his position."I saw what was happening with the company, what was happening with the stock. And I think it's a great thing that he's going back. And when I did speak to him, he is so happy to be going back. He calls it his second term."The US president also praised Huang's family, particularly his wife, while reiterating his confidence in the Nvidia chief."His wife is phenomenal. She's been through a lot. She's a great lady, highly respected by everybody that knows her. His kids likewise, but I just don't know them. But I do know his wife. And she's a phenomenal woman and he's a phenomenal man."Trump further said he believed his intervention would benefit the country and the global technology industry, pointing to the market's recovery after an initial decline."The market feels very good about it. I was a little concerned yesterday when I saw some pretty big dips. And by the end of the day, it was up again. So I think I did a great thing for our country and even for the world."Trump dismisses national security concerns over HuangTrump's defence of Huang comes amid questions within the US intelligence community over potential counterintelligence risks involving Alice Huang, who was previously associated with the Nvidia chief and reportedly had contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security (MSS).Asked how he could be certain Huang did not pose a national security threat when the Justice Department had not conducted a proper investigation, Trump responded, "Based on information and belief. I think he's absolutely fine."When pressed to specify the information supporting his assessment, Trump said, "The information I have, which is a lot of information."He also expressed confidence in Huang's ability to lead Nvidia again, saying, "He's a good man. He's going to do a great job. He's going to do a better job the second time than even in the first, if that's possible."According to a CBS News report, US intelligence officials briefed congressional staffers on Tuesday that China's MSS may have monitored Alice Huang and attempted to obtain information from her after she began an affair with the Nvidia CEO.However, US intelligence agencies have not established the full extent of the matter. They have found no evidence so far that Alice Huang was specifically directed to collect information about Jensen Huang or that she shared information of substantial intelligence value with China, CBS News reported.Citing multiple sources familiar with the discussions, the report said US intelligence agencies had identified Alice Huang's contact with an MSS officer dating back to at least the spring of 2025. These interactions prompted concerns within the intelligence community over possible counterintelligence risks.Congressional staffers were also informed that Kang Wei, believed to be Alice Huang's husband, had deeper connections with the MSS, according to people familiar with the briefing.The two-hour briefing brought together senior analysts from several US intelligence agencies and staff members of the House and Senate Intelligence Committees. It followed Trump's intervention to facilitate Huang's return to Nvidia despite national security reservations reportedly expressed by some of his senior advisers.Rubio had flagged intelligence concernsThe concerns were also outlined in a classified memorandum prepared by Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio in the spring. The document reportedly summarised US intelligence, including intercepted communications involving Alice Huang, and was circulated among senior administration officials to flag potential counterintelligence risks arising from her association with Jensen Huang.Rubio also briefed Trump on the intelligence. The memorandum was shared with several senior officials, including Vice President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and CIA Director John Ratcliffe.Despite requests from both congressional intelligence committees, the classified memorandum was not made available to staffers during Tuesday's briefing, CBS News reported.China has rejected allegations that Alice Huang is a spy.Alice Huang previously held a senior position at Singapore-based firm Megaspeed, which is facing a US investigation over allegations that sensitive American technology may have been diverted to China. The company has denied violating US export control regulations and said Alice Huang left the firm last year.Investigations into possible export control violations involving Megaspeed and another Nvidia chip buyer, Super Micro Computer, are continuing. The FBI has been examining both matters for more than a year, while the Justice Department's National Security Division is overseeing the Megaspeed investigation.Jensen Huang is scheduled to appear on Capitol Hill next week for a private meeting with House lawmakers and is also expected to give public testimony before the Senate Banking Committee, CBS News reported.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut on Thursday seemingly backed Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath, describing him as the highest \"face
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut on Thursday seemingly backed Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath, describing him as the highest "face of Hindutva" and expressing confidence that he would continue to lead the state after the 2027 state assembly elections."If Yogi ji has declared himself (as CM face), it is commendable. He is a capable man, and we too love Yogi ji. Yogi ji is a face of Hindutva that stands at the very top, and if there is no Yogi, there is no UP. If Yogi ji has said this, then he has full confidence that his party will win a majority in Uttar Pradesh and that the majority of MLAs elected will support him," Raut said.Raut's "endorsement" has brought the question of the BJP's chief ministerial face in Uttar Pradesh into sharper focus, particularly after UP deputy CM Keshav Prasad Maurya asserted that a CM would be chosen by newly elected MLAs, rather than naming Adityanath as the party's automatic choice.While Adityanath's position as the BJP's most prominent leader in the state is undisputed, Maurya's remarks have revived speculation over whether the party will project the incumbent CM or leave the decision to its elected MLAs after the polls. The opposition seems to be now capitalising on the contrasting signals within the BJP.What Maurya saidOn Wednesday, Maurya had said the BJP's chief ministerial candidate would be decided by the party's elected MLAs after the Assembly elections, signalling that the party had not yet formally settled on a face for the next polls."BJP's face at the time of elections is the lotus flower, and elections are contested based on the lotus flower. After the elections, when MLAs are elected, their meeting is held, and central observers arrive," Maurya said, according to ANI.Asked whether he could be a contender for the post, Maurya said, "No individual decides this. SP, BSP, and Congress are private limited companies.""We have a system here. Whenever the leader of the legislative party is chosen, central observers come after the election. Whatever happens, you will find out in 2027," he added.Congress piles onMeanwhile, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Thursday targeted the BJP over its performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, crediting voters in Uttar Pradesh with checking the party's electoral ambitions and forcing Prime Minister Narendra Modi to abandon his '400 paar' slogan.Addressing a 'Samvidhan Raksha Sammelan' at the Congress office in Lucknow on Constitution Day, Kharge said the BJP had fallen well short of its target despite Modi repeatedly invoking the slogan during the election campaign."I thank the people of Uttar Pradesh. Prime Minister Narendra Modi used to say in all his speeches, wherever he went, 'Abki Baar, 400 Paar' (this time, more than 400 seats). But did the BJP cross 400 seats? The people sent you (BJP) packing. The people of Uttar Pradesh brought you to your knees. It is because of Uttar Pradesh that Modi is sitting quietly today," Kharge said.The BJP-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA) won 36 of Uttar Pradesh's 80 Lok Sabha seats in the 2024 general elections.Kharge also accused the BJP of allowing its funds to swell while people continued to grapple with inflation, unemployment and rising prices of cooking gas and essential food items. He further claimed that Union Home Minister Amit Shah had reduced his public statements, adding, "I do not know whether the two (Modi and Shah) are getting along or not."In an apparent reference to Adityanath, the Congress president also claimed that another leader in Lucknow had his eyes on the prime minister's chair.The political exchanges come as the Samajwadi Party (SP) and Congress continue discussions over a possible alliance for the 2027 Assembly elections. The SP has offered 26 seats to the Congress in the initial round of negotiations, while the Congress has sought 120 seats and is unwilling to settle for a lower number, according to sources.The SP is seeking to return to power after losing the 2017 and 2022 Assembly elections. articles.summary: Adilabad: Police say father killed 18-year-old daughter before betrothal, staged suicide and rushed cremation; accused Kailash arrested, remanded.
articles.body: HYDERABAD: A day before her betrothal, an 18-year-old woman in Adilabad allegedly told her family that she did not want marry the man they had chosen for her as she was in love with another man.Hours later, her father allegedly smothered her to death while she slept, hanged her body from a roof beam to pass it off as suicide and hurriedly cremated the body before relatives could arrive, police said.Police arrested accused Kailash on Thursday after questioning. The woman, A Kalyani, was killed at the family’s home in Umri village in Adilabad in the early hours of Nov 24, police said.Cops first became suspicious over the haste with which the family conducted the last rites. Narnoor police had received an alert from Umri residents around 8.30 am on Nov 24 about Kalyani’s suspicious death.“By the time our team reached the village, the cremation was almost completed. The woman’s father claimed that she hanged herself at home and they noticed the body at 5.30 am. We became suspicious since the family tried to finish the final rites without waiting for relatives within three hours after her death. Also, in their community, unmarried deceased are buried and not cremated as per custom,” Adilabad district SP Akhil Mahajan said.Umri panchayat secretary B Rajanna had lodged a complaint with Narnoor police a day after her death, stating that Kalyani’s marriage had been fixed and her engagement was scheduled for Nov 25. articles.title: MoD has no email addresses for about half of its reservists
articles.summary: There are an estimated 95,000 reservists but the MoD has only been able to send letters to about 50,000 of them.
articles.body:
The Ministry of Defence (MoD) is urging reservists to update their contact details, after it has emerged it does not have email addresses for about half of them.

The UK has an estimated 95,000 members in its strategic reserve force, which is made up of veterans who can be recalled in exceptional circumstances, but the MoD said it has only been able to send letters to around 50,000.

Open letters have been published on the ministry's website encouraging others to "reconnect".

On Thursday Defence Secretary Wes Streeting confirmed that the MoD had written to ex-military personnel to check their contact details and skills against the backdrop of a rising "threat environment".

His comments were made after The Times and the Telegraph reported that reservists who previously served in the Armed Forces had received letters telling them to prepare to be called up for war.

Streeting told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that this meant should they ever be needed "either for a national disaster here at home or for a more serious threat or conflict elsewhere" then they would "know where our strategic reserve is" and what their skills were.

"I want the country to be alert, not alarmed," he said.

The defence secretary also reiterated the importance of keeping "up to date" with reservists, and ensuring they had access to "further development opportunities".

On the MoD's website, the ministry said it was re-engaging with reservists due to a "more dangerous and unpredictable security environment."

It emphasised that the threshold for being recalled is high and reservists would not be used to fill routine staffing shortages in peacetime.

"It may be considered for serious national emergencies, warlike operations, preparations for war or a major crisis that requires additional military capability," it said.

Earlier this year, former Defence Secretary Lord Robertson said officials were failing to maintain records of military veterans who were entering the reserves.

"The Ministry of Defence at the present moment doesn't even know where most of them are," he said in April.

"So we need to round up those who are available and fit and willing to be able to do it."

Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton has made similar comments, warning in January that the UK did not have "an effective system of tracking and engaging" personnel after they had left the Armed Forces.

articles.title: Meet Pittsburgh's 'Green Bean Man': 76-year-old wakes up at 2:45 am every Thanksgiving to cook 675 pounds of green beans for people in need; has kept the tradition alive for 30 years, saying volunteering gives him more than he gives others
articles.summary: A 76-year-old volunteer in Pittsburgh has continued an unusual Thanksgiving tradition for nearly three decades, preparing hundreds of pounds of green
articles.body: A 76-year-old volunteer in Pittsburgh has continued an unusual Thanksgiving tradition for nearly three decades, preparing hundreds of pounds of green beans for people in need. Known locally as the 'Green Bean Man', Don Waite began his Thanksgiving volunteering at Light of Life Rescue Mission in 1996. On November 26, 2026, he arrived at 2:45 am to prepare 675 pounds of green beans using 13 pounds of butter for the organisation's holiday meal programme. His annual kitchen shift has become a familiar part of the mission's Thanksgiving effort, which provides food to people experiencing homelessness and food insecurity. Despite the early starts and enormous quantities involved, Waite says volunteering has given him more than he feels he has given in return.How Don Waite became Pittsburgh's 'Green Bean Man'Waite's association with the Thanksgiving kitchen began in 1996, when he started volunteering at Light of Life Rescue Mission. Another volunteer initially showed him how to prepare the green beans. When that person was unavailable for a later Christmas meal, Waite was asked to take over the task.He agreed, and what began as a request to help with one meal gradually became an annual commitment. Over the years, the quantity of green beans he prepared grew, and the nickname 'Green Bean Man' became associated with his work.Local reports have documented the tradition across several years. In 2016, WTAE reported that Waite had already spent 20 years preparing green beans for the mission. By 2023, he was reportedly handling around 600 pounds for Thanksgiving.675 pounds of green beans prepared before sunriseFor the 2026 Thanksgiving meal, Waite began work at 2:45 am on November 26. He prepared 675 pounds of green beans, using 13 pounds of butter, at the mission's Ridge Recovery Place on Pittsburgh's North Shore.The Pittsburgh Post-Gazette reported that Waite wore a denim button-down shirt embroidered with his nickname, which he had owned for 25 years. He also joked that he was the only person who enjoyed eating green beans at 4 am.The quantity was part of the mission's wider Thanksgiving food effort, which included hot meals and dinner boxes for people across the Pittsburgh area.'I get more than I give': Why Waite keeps returningFor Waite, the annual kitchen shift is not something he considers a burden. Speaking to WPXI in November 2026, he reflected on his three decades of volunteering and said: "I've never, in 30 years, walked away from here going, 'What a burden.'"He added: "I get more than I give."His remarks capture the personal meaning he attaches to the tradition. While the work involves an early start and preparing food on a large scale, Waite has continued to return because of the satisfaction he finds in helping others.Light of Life's 74-year Thanksgiving traditionLight of Life Rescue Mission has been providing Thanksgiving meals since 1952. Its 2026 holiday programme marked 74 years of serving people in need.The organisation's 2026 Thanksgiving programme included more than 1,200 hot meals, with food served at its Voeghtly Street Shelter and delivered to residents of local high-rise buildings. Around 700 people were expected at the shelter. Separately, 150 volunteers packed 3,000 Thanksgiving meal boxes, each designed to feed a family of eight and collectively reach approximately 24,000 people. The mission expected its overall holiday outreach to provide food to more than 25,000 people during the week.The Pittsburgh-based nonprofit also provides food, shelter and support to people experiencing homelessness, poverty and addiction. Its food pantry distributes groceries, including fresh produce, dairy products, proteins and dry goods, to families facing food insecurity.Rising demand adds urgency to the mission's workThe Thanksgiving effort comes as Light of Life has reported increased demand for food assistance. By October 2026, its pantry had distributed more than 44,000 additional pounds of food compared with the total amount distributed during all of 2025.The organisation's work also includes support for people rebuilding their lives after addiction and those experiencing homelessness. articles.body: Rare rubber boa sightings in British Columbia are uncommon, which made one West Kelowna homeowner’s discovery beside his swimming pool genuinely remarkable. The rubber boa is one of only two boa species native to Canada. Non-venomous, harmless to people and secretive by nature, the snake usually stays underground or hidden beneath cover, which is why seeing one lying out in the open is so unusual. The species ranges as far south as California, with rare sightings reported in Colorado and Alberta, while British Columbia marks its northernmost limit and holds the highest latitude of any boa species in the world.Rubber boa snake found by West Kelowna homeowner in his backyard poolAccording to Castanet, West Kelowna resident Frank Schopp was checking his irrigation system at about eight o’clock on a Wednesday morning in June when he spotted a snake roughly 18 inches (about 46 centimetres) long in a shaded part of his pool patio. It turned out to be a rubber boa, sunning itself beside the water.Schopp told Castanet he scooped the snake up with a shovel and that it “curled up a little bit”. He then moved the animal to a rock pile at the edge of his property.Why expanding development can bring wildlife such as the rubber boa into British Columbia gardensAs per the reports, human-wildlife interactions, expanding development and changing landscapes can make animals more likely to appear where people do not expect them, a point it drew from BBC Future. The report also noted that British Columbia was tracking the species.As neighbourhoods spread into or near natural habitat, the report added, preserving habitat corridors and planning landscapes thoughtfully can help reduce surprise encounters in heavily used human spaces.What to do if you find a rubber boa near your swimming pool or garden in British ColumbiaThe same Yahoo report advised that anyone unsure what a snake is should leave it alone, keep children and pets away, and contact local wildlife or conservation officials if necessary to reduce the risk of a negative outcome.It also suggested checking shaded corners, equipment areas and other tucked-away spots before stepping in, which helps avoid startling an animal that may simply be passing through.You use AI every day. articles.title: Reform UK pledges to scrap hospital parking fees in England
articles.summary: The party says it would compensate NHS trusts for lost fees by charging foreign nationals more for care.
articles.body:
Reform UK is promising to scrap parking fees at NHS hospitals in England for all patients, visitors, and staff if it wins power at the next election.

The party said rising parking charges in recent years were unfair, with some hospitals charging up to £20 a day for parking spots.

It says it would compensate hospital trusts for the £300m they currently get from fees each year by raising more from foreign visitors using the NHS.

The health department said it expected charges to be reasonable, with fees used to maintain facilities or put towards funding health services.

Reform's announcement is part of a broader effort by the party to win credibility on the NHS, as it prepares to appoint someone who has worked in the NHS as its health spokesperson in the coming weeks.

Leader Nigel Farage's previous support for an insurance-based healthcare model has harmed the party's standing on the health service, insiders admit.

The latest policy is also part of a series designed to improve the party's recent struggles in the polls by addressing what Reform see as their perceived weaknesses, on Russia, on defence and now the NHS.

Reform's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick told the BBC the party's spending plans would be set closer to an election, but the party would ensure there would always be "real-terms increases" in funding for the NHS.

Echoing a line traditionally used by British politicians to claim stewardship of the health service, he said: "What we are saying is that the NHS is safe in our hands".

Parking at hospitals in Wales and Scotland is largely free, but NHS trusts in England are allowed to charge and set their own fees and rules.

Government guidance means parking is free for disabled people holding Blue Badges, frequent outpatients, parents of sick children staying overnight and NHS staff working night shifts.

But most visitors are generally expected to pay, along with staff working day shifts.

Reform says its policy to compensate NHS trusts would cost £285m a year to deliver, assuming a £25m annual saving from payment collection costs that would not longer be required.

It plans to recoup lost revenue by charging overseas visitors 200% of the national tariff for NHS services, instead of 150% currently, and extending charges to A&E visits, ambulance services and GP care.

It also says it would make all foreign visitors from countries that do not have reciprocal healthcare arrangements with the UK take out travel insurance covering NHS care, allowing it to "more aggressively collect" money due.

Siva Anandaciva, policy director at the King's Fund health think tank, said parking fees could be a "burden" for those visiting hospitals, but questioned whether Reform's proposals would raise enough to fully compensate trusts.

He said the additional charges on visitors for care would bring extra administration costs, whilst hospitals would need to spend money on systems to ensure free spaces were available to those who need them most.

The experience in Scotland had shown it can also take an "awfully long time" for hospitals to exit contracts with private firms running car pars, he said.

He added: "You might not end up saving as much money as you think".

The health department said it expected fees charged by trusts to be "reasonable and in line with the local area".

"Where charges do apply, the money made is used to maintain facilities, with surplus income put back into the NHS to benefit both staff and patients," a spokesperson added.

In response to parliamentary questions earlier this year, the department also argued fees were a "significant control mechanism" to manage capacity given the limited number of car parking spaces available.

articles.title: Leaders clash in final Spain election debate as housing dominates run-in
articles.summary: The struggle many face in buying a home has been the biggest issue of a bitter campaign.
articles.body:
Spain's main party leaders have made their last pitch to voters in a fractious final TV debate that focused heavily on the country's housing crisis.

Spaniards go to the ballot box on Sunday, with opinion polls suggesting Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will fail to extend his eight years in office.

The debate on Thursday night marked the culmination of a campaign, which has been defined by the din of house keys being jangled in symbolic protest, rather than any carefully crafted words of politicians.

The struggle many face in opening the door to an affordable home has led to demonstrations filling plazas across the country.

Alberto Núñez Feijóo of the conservative People's Party (PP), who is poised to replace Sánchez, told viewers he would build a million new homes.

PP, which is narrowly projected to be the largest party, is poised to form a government with the far-right Vox party which is polling in third place.

This would be the first time the far right has assumed power at the national level in Spain's 50 years of democracy following the Franco dictatorship.

Vox's leader Santiago Abascal told the debate only he cared about those who had the greatest housing need.

Ada Colau, who heads a left-wing coalition of four small left-wing parties called Broad Front, said taxing rich and exploitative landlords was urgently required.

Rejecting criticism that he had failed to tackle the country's housing problem, Sanchez talked up his recent emergency measures designed to protect tenants and cap rents.

Spanish elections: What you need to know and what's at stake

Sparking the protests in September was the eviction – and subsequent death in hospital – of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal (no relation to Santiago). She could not afford a tripling of her rent in Madrid.

But it is Spain's third city, Valencia, that is at the heart of what many call a full-blown housing crisis.

"We want to live together but we look at the prices of property and it's impossible," says 25-year-old Nuria Cifuentes from the city.

She and her boyfriend Miguel Martínez work as sports journalists but are still living with their respective families because of the high cost of renting a flat, even with their combined salaries.

"Half of what we earn would go on rent of more than 1,000 euros a month," Miguel, 26, says.

We meet the couple outside Valencia's futuristic science museum, whose distinctive design is often compared to the skeleton of a whale.

This coastal location has witnessed the biggest rise in rent prices of any major Spanish city over the past half a decade, according to official data from the INE, the national statistics office.

One study from the city's Polytechnic University put the increase at 78% between 2020 and 2025.

Sánchez called a snap election after Congress rejected his emergency housing reforms.

A revised version was later pushed through a parliamentary standing committee – restricting evictions and capping rent rises – but opponents say he has had eight years to sort the problem and has resolutely failed.

Nuria and Miguel say the soaring cost of housing means that life is on pause for them, as they're unable to make concrete plans for the future.

"Maybe we want to have kids, maybe we want to actually buy somewhere, but there are so many unknowns that all I see is a black expanse," Nuria says.

"The problem here is that our salaries are very low and life is very expensive."

The wider cost of living is the second most important issue for Spaniards, according to numerous surveys carried out during this election period.

Wages failing to catch up with rising prices – despite Spain's GDP growing faster than the three bigger EU countries, Germany, France and Italy – is another reason why Sánchez's PSOE party is only sitting in second place, according to final opinion polls.

Feijóo is said to be most likely to form the next government with the support of the far-right Vox under its leader Santiago Abascal.

Having called access to housing a "vital emergency", Feijóo wants to cut taxes for under-40s buying their first home and scrap the Socialists' housing law.

On housing, Vox has gone further than PSOE and PP, promising to prioritise Spaniards over foreigners for social housing and housing aid, as well as other welfare benefits.

On immigration, identified as the third most important issue, Vox advocates deportations for criminals from abroad and, most controversially, a policy of remigration for foreign nationals who "do not contribute to Spain".

Opponents of Vox say those who have arrived legally and live and work peacefully risk being forced out.

But 30-year-old Daniel, who is currently unemployed, says he is ready to give his vote to Vox for the first time.

"First of all, it's immigration. It's bad in Spain today – that's why I'm going further to the right," he says.

"The left helps those who don't work, but we need people who work and contribute. We need to give less aid to people who come from abroad and don't contribute."

Daniel says taxes need to come down immediately.

"We are almost being charged to just breathe at the moment," he says.

We meet Daniel coming out of a shopping centre. We explain that other people we met in the previous hour who told us they support Vox did not want to give their name or be photographed.

Is he proud to be voting far right, or does he have concerns about his choice?

"I'll say it like it is… I've always been centre right but have gone to the extreme right… I've decided to choose nationalism."

Spain's control of its borders was criticised by 22 of its 26 EU partners in the summer, in a rebuke to Sánchez.

In July more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory of Ceuta in just two days.

Sánchez has argued the foreign workforce is essential to Spain's economic growth, and in April announced plans to give half a million undocumented migrants legal status.

In the final days of the campaign, Sánchez has made a flurry of new spending announcements amounting to billions of euros, promising wage rises in the public sector, higher pensions and discounted transport.

Twenty-year-old student María García says she welcomes the promises but asks why they have come so late in the day.

"The Socialist party have been in power for eight years and now suddenly, during the election campaign, they are passing a lot of progressive laws – which I agree with – but isn't that hypocritical?" she says.

"I don't really have a choice but to vote for them, but come on – you had eight years to do all this!"

Maria's sentiments chime with those of her boyfriend German Martinez, 18.

I put it to them that nearly a fifth of Spaniards are said to be choosing Vox and a number of studies say it's set to be the top choice of first-time voters.

"I believe Spain is stepping into the lion's den because we are scared of the dogs outside. We need to be careful," she says.

"People need to inform themselves – just listen to what these guys say. That 20% of Spanish people agree with them really scares me."

Sánchez will be hoping that fear among the undecided of a national government that includes Vox will save him.

He is a great political survivor, but even if his party wins the most votes he has no obvious path to build a majority.

The man who called a snap election over housing now faces his own eviction - from office.

Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election

articles.title: Inside Saudi Arabia, Houthi attacks test kingdom's image of security
articles.summary: Despite the strikes, markets and restaurants in Riyadh remain busy as residents express trust in the government to protect them.
articles.body:
Ten days after fleeing his home in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, Abu Khalil is selling socks on the streets of Riyadh.

"I walked out of Sanaa, I crossed the front line," he says, adding that he "hitched a ride into Saudi Arabia".

Families in Yemen are "struggling to provide for [their] children", he says, as he tries to earn enough to send some money home.

He asks us not to use his full name because his wife and four children are still in Sanaa, and he is frightened of what might happen to them if he is identified speaking out against the Houthis. "I ran away from the Houthis but I couldn't bring my family with me. May God protect them," he says.

Backed by Iran, the armed group has controlled much of northern Yemen since a civil war erupted more than a decade ago. It is fighting the internationally recognised government, which is supported by neighbouring Saudi Arabia.

And Saudi cities, such as Riyadh, are now coming under regular drone and missile attacks from the very group Abu Khalil fled.

An informal ceasefire in Yemen unravelled in July, and since the fighting escalated, the Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia. They have said they were retaliating against deadly Saudi air strikes in Yemen and what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled territory.

One Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured more than 300 - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in years.

Having been granted rare permission to report from Riyadh, we spoke to locals, including Majid, a 25-year-old engineer who works for the Saudi state oil company Aramco. He was passing through the airport that day, rushing for a flight to Jeddah for a religious pilgrimage.

He says he was watching a mother push her children in a pushchair when the terminal was hit.

He remembers seeing a man covered in blood. "I went to him in shock, asking him, 'Are you OK?'" He says he saw injured and unconscious passengers being taken to the airport's first aid clinic.

"Some of them, I still don't know whether they were alive or not."

The experience left him shaken. "The threat is real," he tells me. "But I will not let the Houthis make me feel unsafe in my own country."

The airport attack was far from an isolated incident. BBC analysis of data from the US-based Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled), a non-profit organisation, which collects data on political violence and protests around the world, identified 274 attacks on Saudi Arabia in almost five months between 1 July and 25 November.

According to Acled, most of these were intercepted, but at least 41 were not and in some cases debris from the interception also caused damage.

Drones featured in almost two-thirds of the attacks, while ballistic missiles were used in more than half, according to the data.

In the previous five months, Acled recorded just one Houthi attack on the country.

Backed by Iran, the Houthis have developed an increasingly sophisticated arsenal, dramatically extending their ability to repeatedly strike deep in Saudi territory.

For years, Houthi attacks were largely concentrated near the Yemeni border, with Riyadh targeted far less frequently. But since the collapse of the unofficial ceasefire, the Saudi capital, more than 700km (430 miles) away from the Yemeni border, is now coming under regular attack.

As well as the airport, oil installations and prominent buildings in the capital have been in danger.

Saudi Arabia has spent billions transforming its cities, attracting international investment and presenting itself to the world as a safe place to live, work and visit - the attacks have put this promise to the test.

Two prominent skyscrapers have been hit in Riyadh's financial district this month.

Eleven people were injured in a strike on the Public Investment Fund (PIF) Tower, which is the tallest in Saudi Arabia and is the headquarters of the country's sovereign wealth fund. The other was the Aramco building, home to the state oil company.

As we drove past the Aramco tower, the damage was a clear reminder of the threat facing the kingdom.

But within days, the building's exterior had been completely repaired, any visible sign of the attack erased. It was perhaps a reflection of Saudi Arabia's determination to project an image of stability and business as usual, even as the attacks continue.

The government has condemned "terrorist attacks targeting civilian and economic facilities" and said it would "take all necessary measures" to defend itself.

Even so, flights to the capital have been severely disrupted by the strikes, which have also targeted other locations, such as Medina and the airport in the eastern city of Dammam.

Many passengers travelling to Riyadh are being routed through different airports and making the final leg of the journey on land.

The flight we took to Dammam was almost empty. Riyadh's streets tell a different story, though.

Restaurants are bustling, families browse at shopping centres and people go about their evenings seemingly undeterred by the threat overhead.

But getting people to speak openly about the conflict is difficult in a country where strict censorship laws and restrictions on freedom of expression make many wary of talking to the media.

Many of those who did speak to us expressed confidence in their country's ability to protect them. At a busy market, Badr says the airport attack was worrying, but life has quickly returned to normal. "I sleep comfortably," he says, praising the country's security forces.

Another man, Rashid, gestures towards the stalls around us: "The market is booming. People are buying and selling, going about their business. Everything is good."

But the normality he describes is periodically disturbed by a sudden buzz on the phone with an alert warning of an incoming attack. Then come the loud booms of air defences intercepting missiles and drones overhead.

We experienced one at 04:00 one morning, and the knowledge that not every attack is being intercepted can leave people afraid.

British expatriate Alex Malouf, who has lived in Saudi Arabia on and off since 2006, says he worries about the psychological impact on his 11-year-old daughter, who has experienced security alerts while at school.

"There have been times when my daughter has said, 'Daddy, I'm scared.' It has been something which I think has shaken our reality."

Despite the attacks, Abu Khalil says he feels much safer in Saudi Arabia than at home in Yemen where fighting has intensified.

The Houthis' renewed offensive in western Yemen has seen the group capture territory along the Red Sea coast and threaten strategic routes towards the southern city of Aden, the government's temporary base.

The fighting has also intensified around Taiz , a government-controlled city that has endured years of siege and conflict.

Road closures resulting from the latest Houthi siege there have severely restricted deliveries of essential supplies, leaving more than 800,000 people cut off from humanitarian assistance, according to the UN children's agency Unicef. Food and fuel that can be found have shot up in price.

More than 360,000 people have been forced from their homes in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). And the UN Human Rights Office has verified 323 civilian casualties since then, including 76 killed, with children accounting for half of the dead.

A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has responded to the Houthi advances and attacks on the kingdom with intensified air strikes, adding to the dangers faced by civilians. One strike in Sanaa earlier this month killed 44 people, according to Houthi authorities. Saudi Arabia says these operations were to protect the Yemeni population and global trade from the Houthis.

Saudi-led bombing campaigns during the earlier years of the war killed thousands of civilians and devastated homes, hospitals and schools.

The Houthis have also inflicted enormous suffering on civilians through shelling, missile and ground attacks on government-held territory, as well as repression in areas under their control.

Abu Khalil hopes that he will soon be able to bring his wife and children over to Saudi Arabia, away from the dangers in Sanaa, and says he "will not go back until the Houthis are gone".

Additional reporting by Jasmin Dyer and Ahmed Nour

articles.title: Sussex search dog given animal OBE after death
articles.summary: Cain the border collie joined Search Dogs Sussex in 2013, and has been given a PDSA Order of Merit.
articles.body:
A search and rescue dog who helped to save missing people for11 years has bee given an award dubbed the "OBE for animals" two months after his death.

Cain, who joined Search Dogs Sussex in June 2013 at 18-months-old, helped to save people across difficult terrain and in difficult scenarios, going from being the group's youngest recruit to its longest serving dog.

The border collie has now posthumously been given the PDSA Order of Merit, an award which recognises the "special relationship between animals and humans", the charity says.

Cain's handler, Steve Ball, said: "He was an extraordinary dog, not just in his work but as part of our family. He will always be very special to us."

He added: "Cain was my search dog for more than a decade, and I had him since he was just eight weeks old. Even from a very young age, there was something special about him. He always had that extra edge.

"He absolutely deserves this award. He gave 11 years of exceptional service to the Sussex community, and I couldn't be prouder that he has been recognised in this way."

Cain retired from service in January 2024, but died in September before he could be presented with the award.

In total, 43 dogs and 13 horses have been given the Order of Merit award since it was established, including Cain.

Sussex Police Chief Constable Jo Shiner said she was "incredibly proud" of Cain, adding that the partnership between Ball and the border collie "has made a huge contribution to protecting the public".

PDSA director general Jan McLoughlin said: "Cain's service, which spanned over a decade, demonstrates the commitment, capability and vital contribution of search dogs in saving human life, making Cain a very worthy recipient of the PDSA Order of Merit. He will be greatly missed."

articles.title: Whitehaven's Hope Haven hub issuing 'nature prescriptions'
articles.summary: The Hope Haven hub is encouraging people to step outside in an effort to improve their well-being.
articles.body:
People struggling with their mental health are being encouraged to connect with nature on their doorstep.

Hope Haven, in Whitehaven, west Cumbria, opened in March as one of six pilot centres across the country dedicated to tackling problems before they escalate.

It has now joined forces with the RSPB to issue "nature prescriptions", which see people encouraged to visit a number of places in the area, such as the local harbour, sand dunes at Ravenglass and Walkmill Community Woodland at Moresby.

Clinical manager Barbara Slater said the scheme was "another tool" to add to the hub's range of interventions.

Visitors to Hope Haven, located in a former bank building in the town centre, are able to discuss their concerns with mental health professionals without needing a referral.

Slater said the nature prescriptions, a series of suggestions for local walks and activities contained in a booklet, were "a great way to gently introduce nature and well-being into people's lives".

"Being close to the Lake District, people often think that to go out in nature you need special equipment and boots," she said.

"We purposefully tailored it to Copeland, putting suggestions in for places that can be reached by public transport and most are free.

"That was really important because we want people to feel they're not excluded."

Other featured locations include Whitehaven's Castle Park, Seascale seafront and St Bees Head, home to a breeding site for guillemots.

Not all suggestions contained in the booklet required travel, however.

"It can be as simple as being outside and breathing the air," Slater said.

"Another is to look at raindrops on a window and watch the water roll down. It's about connecting with something much bigger than ourselves."

Hope Haven is the first organisation in Cumbria to take part in the scheme.

Staff training and the production of the booklets has been funded with £5,500 secured via partner organisations including the NHS, National Lottery and West Cumbria Rivers Trust.

Sarah Walker, nature and well-being manager at RSPB England, said the charity's trials had shown "even taking a moment or two to notice nature can boost mental and physical health".

"So many people face a whole range of pressures in their lives and nature could provide a way to help them through and find a moment of joy in their day," she added.

More than 5,000 people have visited Hope Haven since its opening with that number prompting conflicting emotions, Slater said.

"We're very busy because the community is coming to see us, but there's also a sadness because it shows there are struggles with a range of issues - anxiety, feeling in crisis, debt and alcohol problems.

"We try to help people in those really dark places."
