articles.title: RSPCA launches pop-up pet food bank in Sheffield
articles.summary: RSPCA hands out food, vet vouchers, cat litter and toys to pet owners struggling with bills.
articles.body:
At Burngreave Foodbank in Sheffield, a queue of worried people are here not to collect groceries for themselves, but food for their pets.

The RSPCA has launched a pop-up food bank to hand out cat litter, veterinary vouchers and pet toys as well as food.

Many of the dog and cat owners using the service say that rising bills are leaving them in fear they will not be able to care for their beloved companions.

John Paul Feely, 59, has four cats and a dog, and currently spends £35 a month on them.

"At the moment we're facing rises in fuel costs, food costs and you've got to make a choice at some point, can we look after the animals?" he says.

Feely worries that unexpected vet bills as well as the day-to-day expenses could tip him over the edge when his energy bill goes up in January.

Energy bills will soar by 26% for millions of households in January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war.

A typical bill will increase by about £37 a month in the first three months of the new year.

The government will pay millions of households £100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity.

Feely lives with his partner and explains that they are already making tough decisions about "turning the lights out and not putting the heating on".

He is able to take home food supplies and a dog chew toy.

As food bank volunteers offer tea and coffee to those waiting in the queue, Angela Gillot accepts a small dog jacket from the RSPCA stall with a smile.

She explains with a tear in her eye that since becoming unemployed she has felt the pinch of rising bills.

The RSPCA estimates that the cost of keeping a small dog like a Jack Russell could be up to £209 a month.

Energy costs going up next year "will affect everything," Gillot admits, as she describes how she and her dog huddle up under a blanket to keep warm.

"We do love these pets. We're a pet-loving nation aren't we? But it's getting harder.

"When I got my dogs I was working, so I try my best, but the price of food, especially what's of quality, I just really can't afford it.

"It's not often you go to these places and they think about your pets," the 58-year-old says.

Tricia Watts, the upbeat assistant manger at Burngreave Foodbank, is enthusiastic about the support from the RSPCA.

She explains that while the food bank works with people in food poverty, it cannot always help people with animal care as it relies on donations.

She has seen demand increase, and donations fall, in the seven years she has worked at the food bank.

"I think pets are so important to people. If people are going through hard times, they're still important and they don't want to lose them."

Growing bills are of particular concern to exotic animal owners as many birds, reptiles and fish must be kept in carefully maintained conditions that are often energy-intensive.

Carl Chandler runs Sustainable Aquatics in Rotherham. He says rising energy prices have had a "gigantic" impact on his business.

Chandler caveats that fish are one of the most wallet-friendly pets.

"To run a tropical fish tank you're looking less than a cup of coffee a week."

Other species, however, require specialist equipment to replicate their natural habitats.

"Reptiles, frogs and amphibians are incredibly expensive to heat because you need UV bulbs and to keep the right humidity."

Back in Burngreave, the pop-up event has managed to give away as much as 50kg of food, the equivalent of more than 100 tins, to pet owners in need.

Sometimes, of course, owners find the challenge simply too much, and give their pets up for rehoming.

"We've seen heartbreaking examples across the country of people leaving notes with animals saying they just can't afford them any more," Chris O'Brien, a spokesperson for the RSPCA, says.

"The cost of giving crisis has put new levels of pressure on us in terms of animals coming in quicker than we can rehome them.

"As these cost of living bombshells keep coming, unfortunately it's going to be a continued difficult time for animal owners across the region."

articles.title: EU leaders fail to bridge budget splits as talks stall
articles.summary: Aid for Ukraine was among the disputes as EU members hope to conclude talks by the end of the year.
articles.body:
European Union (EU) leaders have deferred negotiations on its long-term budget after tensions surfaced over the bloc's spending priorities and aid for Ukraine.

Tense talks on the 2028-34 budget ended after 12 hours on Thursday at a summit in Brussels, with some members walking out of negotiations that will resume in December.

Divisions were largely split along the lines of countries, including France and Italy, wanting to approve a higher-spending proposal against those advocating for financial restraint, with Germany chief among them.

Many members want the budget locked in ahead of several high-stakes elections held across Europe in 2027, including in France.

Countries remain divided over a proposal to provide Ukraine with an additional loan of €45bn (£37.6bn), split between non-military and military funding.

Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Hungary have objected to the loan, but German Chancellor Frederich Merz said uniform EU agreement was a condition for approving the broader budget.

"I stand by my view that aid for Ukraine must be supported by the European Union as a whole," Merz told reporters.

"The European Union comprises of 27 member states, not 23 or 24."

Bulgaria, which previously opposed the plan, said it would agree to fund part of the loan that commits non-military financial support to Kyiv, marking a small sign of progress emerging from the special summit of the European Council.

EU members have been wrangling over the long-term budget after the European Commission submitted a €2tn proposal earlier this year, with some countries objecting to high levels of spending.

Those advocating higher spending want the funds to future-proof industries such as farming and invest in regional development. Fiscally cautious countries want to avoid amassing ballooning debt.

Thursday's talks were set up by the European Council to unblock the impasse, with a proposal to reduce spending by approximately €220bn to €230bn.

Under the current proposal, the budget totals €1.582tn, which includes €140bn to repay pandemic-era borrowing.

Four countries wanting to rein in the budget, including Denmark and Austria, walked out of negotiations after several hours of meetings.

Merz said there was "new movement" towards reducing the size of the EU budget, though he added "we are not there yet" when he confirmed that a new round of negotiations would not take place in Brussels on Friday.

European budgets requires approval from all 27 countries, with each country effectively holding veto power.

French President Emmanuel Macron said it would be a "strategic mistake" to lower long-term spending.

France's forthcoming presidential election came into focus during the EU budget talks, with frontrunner Marine Le Pen calling the talks an "underhanded political manoeuvring to thwart the democratic will of the French people".

Last month, Le Pen announced she would significantly reduce French aid to Ukraine and EU contributions if she were to win the presidency.

Macron addressed Le Pen's remarks on the sidelines of the Brussels summit, saying: "It is an odd kind of arrogance to behave as if she is already in charge of France's destiny because, as things stand, she has not been elected."

Once the talks concluded, the European Council announced a two-day summit on 17 and 18 December would revive budget negotiations.

Spanish economist Pablo Hernández de Cos was also named as the next President of the European Central Bank, replacing Christine Lagarde from February 2027.

articles.title: Chris Mason: Immigration stats are down but will that be the end of the issue?
articles.summary: Net migration falling to the tens of thousands is a landmark moment in our collective national conversation about immigration, says Chris Mason.
articles.body:
Net migration falling to the tens of thousands is a landmark moment in our collective national conversation about immigration over the last couple of decades.

There is a simple reason for this. We have had years and years strewn with the litter of politicians promising to cut net migration to under 100,000 annually.

In the latter decades of the last century, net migration was broadly net zero. Sometimes more folk left than arrived. But, around the time that I first arrived as a reporter in Westminster in 2004, the story was changing and would change rapidly.

I have followed every twist, turn, argument and campaign since, both from Parliament and from Brussels.

On 1 May 2004, the European Union expanded hugely, from 15 to 25 members, the biggest expansion in its history.

The bloc's population grew by 74 million people overnight as countries including Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia and what was then the Czech Republic signed up.

And remember, a core plank of EU membership is freedom of movement: the right to travel, live and work anywhere in the club.

Transitional controls on workers from these former communist states could be applied at the time, but the then-Labour government led by Tony Blair chose not to.

The consequences of that decision were as substantial as they were consequential.

Ministers had predicted a minimal impact. But net migration cranked up.

Crucially, this began to ground arguments about sovereignty in the swirling debates about the UK's membership of the EU.

At the time I was a Europe correspondent based in Brussels and a frequent visitor to the European Parliament in Strasbourg.

The UK Independence Party, led by Nigel Farage, were on the rise. But Eurosceptics would tell me privately that their deeply held concerns about the loss of sovereignty, of power, to EU institutions had been a hard sell to many back home. It was an argument, regardless of its merits or otherwise, that felt theoretical and intellectual to many, rather than practical and grounded in day-to-day concerns.

But that changed for many given the scale of immigration people could see.

Plenty of places, particularly beyond the big cities, felt the rapidity of change. Immigration took on a greater political salience.

Should all control over migration be re-imported to Westminster? Such was the growing strength of feeling among many, a sequence of prime ministers began promising to reduce net migration to the tens of thousands.

David Cameron made the promise. The Conservative election manifesto in 2010 harked back to those numbers before the turn of the century. "We will take steps to take net migration back to the levels of the 1990s – tens of thousands a year, not hundreds of thousands."

Five years later, Cameron renewed the promise, in the Conservative manifesto of 2015. The party would "keep our ambition of delivering annual net migration in the tens of thousands, not the hundreds of thousands," it read.

By 2017, Theresa May was prime minister and while the UK had voted for Brexit, it hadn't happened yet. In the Conservative manifesto that year, she promised "controlled, sustainable migration, with net migration down to the tens of thousands."

At the 2019 general election, Boris Johnson was in Downing Street. He didn't repeat the tens of thousands promise, post Brexit, instead arguing for an "Australian-style points-based immigration system" and, crucially, that "overall numbers will come down."

They didn't. Instead, they soared by almost a million – a giant spike on the graph of recent net migration, branded by his critics as the "Boriswave."

Johnson argued that Brexit would mean Westminster would take back control of migration, as leaving the European Union would mean the end of freedom of movement among the member states.

And yes, Brexit did repatriate that power. But this delivered choices, not a guaranteed outcome that the numbers would fall. And Johnson's choices led instead to a spectacular rise.

It took Rishi Sunak's government and the then-Home Secretary Sir James Cleverly to substantially change the rules and so limit the number of visas granted. The incoming Labour government in 2024 inherited these rules and kept them.

The question now, with the net migration number now in the tens of thousands, is whether immigration will now shrivel as a topic of widespread worry.

How migration feels can be influenced by world view and wealth, politics and geography. Let's take just one aspect of it: the number of asylum seekers being housed in Scotland has increased by 20% over the past year, despite a fall in numbers across the UK as a whole. Glasgow remains the council area with the largest number of people in asylum accommodation in the UK, and there have been increases in areas from Aberdeen to North Lanarkshire which buck the UK-wide trend.

And a lower net figure also does not necessarily mean that the scale of immigration and emigration are low. Large but similar numbers merely serve to almost cancel each other out, numerically. The underlying official statistics set out that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June, while 661,000 emigrated.

But just as previous political choices still have consequences now, a persistently low net migration number, depending on who is coming and going, could have consequences in the future. Take Andy Burnham's desire to shake up social care in England, a sector traditionally reliant on arrivals from overseas for much of its workforce. How might it cope? It's one of many potential questions for the future.

For now, as we examine this latest set of statistics, many will reflect that we have collectively as a country – if not everyone individually - exuded an anguish, sometimes an anger at the scale of immigration. It has been one of the standout demographic, social and so political issues of recent times. Perhaps now that conversation turns to a new chapter.

articles.title: Hero Jack Russell gets PDSA Gold Medal for saving her Birmingham owner after a fall
articles.summary: Holly the Jack Russell repeatedly ran for help and led rescuers to where her owner lay after a fall.
articles.body:
Brave Holly the Jack Russell has been awarded the equivalent of the George Cross for animals after helping to save her owner when he had a serious fall in freezing conditions.

In a scene reminiscent of the TV show Lassie, the terrified terrier ran repeatedly between the Birmingham alleyway where owner Nigel Whatmore had fallen, to a nearby footpath to try to attract attention.

Eventually a couple spotted her strange behaviour and she led them to where her owner lay. They gave first aid and called an ambulance.

Whatmore does not remember the incident and said he "dreads to think what would have happened" if Holly had not been there, adding "she really is my guardian angel".

Holly has now been awarded the PDSA Gold Medal which is the top animal award in the country, rewarding civilian acts of bravery and exceptional devotion to duty.

The award ceremony will take place on Friday.

Whatmore, from Birmingham, said the pair had been out on a morning walk in January and he had not realised the conditions were so icy.

He said the section of the alleyway where he fell could not easily be seen from the road and there was a possibility he could have remained undiscovered for several hours if Holly had not leapt into action.

He suffered a head injury, broken ribs, a damaged shoulder and blood loss as a result of the fall.

Whatmore said: "We later discovered the fall had affected my heart. I was incredibly lucky."

He added that one minute he was looking at the alleyway and the next minute he was in the back of an ambulance with his wife, Laura.

Whatmore said Holly must have been terrified "but stepped up to the mark and did what she needed to do".

"It's just incredible," he said. "She must have been so stressed, but she never gave up. It's the sort of thing you expect to see in films, not something you ever imagine happening to you.

"I honestly don't know what I would have done without her. For her to be awarded the PDSA Gold Medal is unbelievable. It's one of the biggest honours, and we are so incredibly proud of her."

PDSA director general Jan McLoughlin said: "The PDSA Gold Medal is the highest animal honour for life-saving devotion to duty in civilian life.

"Holly's determination, loyalty and instinct make her a very worthy recipient."

articles.title: From Pokhran to partnership: Strobe Talbott’s Indian legacy
articles.summary: TOI Correspondent from Washington: Strobe Talbott, who died on Thursday at 80, belonged to a vanishing breed of American diplomats for whom foreign policy
articles.body: TOI Correspondent from Washington: Strobe Talbott, who died on Thursday at 80, belonged to a vanishing breed of American diplomats for whom foreign policy was as much an exercise in understanding other countries as in advancing their own, a principle that is anathema in the crass MAGA era. Brilliant, cerebral, and possessed of an almost old-fashioned faith in dialogue, he helped accomplish something that, in the summer of 1998, seemed improbable: turning one of the worst crises in US-India relations into an opening for one of Washington’s most consequential strategic partnerships. Indeed, his most enduring diplomatic achievement was not a “deal” he signed or a war he “solved.” It was something more elemental: helping two countries that had spent decades talking past each other to begin talking to each other – respectfully.The story began in the unforgiving aftermath of the Shakti nuclear tests in May 1998, when the Clinton administration reacted with fury to what it saw as India’s imprudence. Sanctions followed, relations deteriorated, and the U.S pressed New Delhi to abandon its nuclear ambitions, sign the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT) and accept the existing international non-proliferation architecture that would cap and roll back its nuclear program. India, under PM Vajpayee, was equally determined not to surrender what it regarded as an indispensable security imperative.Into this diplomatic minefield stepped Talbott, then Deputy Secretary of State -- also previously a Bill Clinton homie at Oxford and a former Time correspondent in Moscow -- and Jaswant Singh, India's principal interlocutor and subsequently External Affairs Minister. What followed was an extraordinary diplomatic marathon, stretching from 1998 to 2000, involving 14 meetings in seven countries, difficult arguments, private exchanges, family dinners in each others’ homes, and, eventually, a degree of mutual trust that neither side could have anticipated. It was a relationship that transcended the negotiating table.The talks did not produce the treaty (CTBT) Washington initially wanted, nor did it accept the American premise that India’s nuclear status was negotiable. But Talbott understood that diplomacy need not always end in agreement to be consequential. In an interview with this correspondent in January 1999, ahead of his eighth round of talks in New Delhi, he described his exchanges with Singh as an exercise in the “art of the possible.” He also revealed that Clinton himself was the primary driver in the effort to repair ties, having read British Indian history as a Rhodes scholar at Oxford, and he was among the first to recognize India’s tech promise because of the y2k issue.Among the books scattered on the table in his office was Jaswant Singh’s “Defending India,” revealing that he was not merely negotiating with New Delhi; he was trying to understand it. Indeed, in Singh, he met an equally formidable diplomat, and the two men developed a friendship rooted in mutual respect, shared intellectual curiosity and an appreciation of each other's national compulsions. Their discussions were not confined to nuclear warheads, missile trajectories and non-proliferation benchmarks. They ranged across history, philosophy, international affairs and the larger question of how two democracies, with very different strategic experiences, could learn to trust each other.The significance of their engagement became apparent during the 1999 Kargil conflict, when Washington took a firm position against Pakistan's military adventurism, their talks aiding better American understanding of India's security concerns. Clinton's landmark visit to India in March 2000 was another milestone. The two countries were no longer simply managing a nuclear disagreement; they were on track for a substantially different relationship.The transformation would take several more years, with the Bush administration's decision to pursue nuclear cooperation with India, culminating in the landmark 2005 nuclear deal, being the crowning moment of this process. But it was the diplomatic groundwork laid by Talbott and Singh that helped establish the proposition that India's nuclear status could be accommodated within a broader strategic partnership rather than remain an eternal obstacle to it.For Talbott, the India engagement was also personal. His affection and admiration for Singh were evident long after both men had left office. When Jaswant Singh died in August 2020, Talbott's tribute was among the most touching. “Extraordinary man, wise and principled servant for his country and the world, brave soldier, honorable statesman, diplomat of finesse and effectiveness, author of wide scope, proud, loved, and loving husband and father, and friend. RIP.” he wrote. Well might every word apply to him.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A 1997 cargo spill sent nearly 5 million LEGO pieces into the sea; more than 25 years later, Cornwall beachcombers were still finding the old sea-creature and pirate toys
articles.summary: Explore how a massive 1997 cargo spill continues to wash LEGO pieces ashore in Cornwall, revealing the long-lasting impact of plastic pollution on marine life.
articles.body: Cornwall in South West England is known for its coastline, but some beachcombers there have been finding more than shells. Decades after they were lost at sea, tiny plastic octopuses, divers, flippers and other LEGO pieces keep washing up on the sand. A University of Plymouth study published in 2020 estimated a LEGO brick could take between 100 and 1,300 years to decompose in the ocean. The pieces are a small, colourful reminder of how long plastics can last once they reach the water.The day a rogue wave hit the Tokio ExpressOn 13 February 1997, a cargo ship named Tokio Express was travelling from Rotterdam in the Netherlands to New York. About 20 miles from the shore, an unexpected 20-foot wave tipped the ship. In total, there were 62 containers that fell off into the sea. The ship was carrying 4,756,940 LEGO pieces and, ironically, most of the kits were themed around sea creatures. Other lost cargo included 10,000 disposable lighters, super glue and other dangerous chemicals. This incident came to be known as the Great LEGO Spill.The beachcombers who keep finding the toysSince the spill, collectors have been searching for rare items such as octopuses and green dragons. Tracey Williams, a Cornwall beachcomber and environmental campaigner, has been documenting the spill for years on the LEGO Lost at Sea Facebook, Instagram and X. She has also written a book, Adrift: The Curious Tale of LEGO Lost at Sea. Little plastic flowers and mini divers’ flippers are frequently seen on the shore. According to a 2014 BBC report, 3,178,807 of the 4,756,940 pieces on board were light enough to float. Those are the most common items found on 40 beaches in Cornwall. In 2017, a local resident, Rob Arnold, and 12 other volunteers collected about 6 million pieces of microplastic from a beach near his home. Two decades after the ship tipped, they found 240 LEGO divers’ flippers among the plastic.What the research foundThe Plymouth paper, titled ‘Weathering and persistence of plastic in the marine environment: Lessons from LEGO,’ was published in Environmental Pollution in 2020, and Tracey Williams is one of its authors. The team compared 50 washed-up bricks donated by beach cleaners in Cornwall with 50 identical bricks which had never left their boxes. They used X-ray fluorescence to analyse the chemical makeup of the plastic.Depending on the brick, the researchers estimated full breakdown could take anywhere from 100 to 1,300 years. Each brick that was washed up was assumed to have been lost around the time it was purchased, and so the figures are estimates rather than precise dates. In comments to Live Science, Williams said that the pieces that sank, as well as those that floated, give insight into how far plastic drifts both on the surface and along the seabed. It also sheds light on what happens as it breaks down.Why a toy spill still mattersPlastic can last in the sea for hundreds of years. As it breaks down, it can release chemicals that may affect the reproductive system of animals. The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) says at least 14 million tons of plastic enter the ocean every year, and it accounts for 80% of all marine debris from surface waters to the deep-sea sediments. The same IUCN brief notes that marine species often eat plastic debris or get tangled in it, causing injuries and death. At the upper end of the study’s estimates, a brick could last for 1,300 years, so the spill’s effects may remain for future generations.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: One plant, 10 expressions: How Indian tea makers use oxidation, plucking and processing to create dramatically different flavours
articles.summary: Tea is so woven into the fabric of Indian life that it’s easy to forget how recently chai became a national habit.
articles.body: Tea is so woven into the fabric of Indian life that it’s easy to forget how recently chai became a national habit. India’s commercial tea industry began in the 1830s when the East India Company began to develop plantations in Assam in an effort to make Britain less dependent on Chinese tea. Tea was not a wholly new thing to the region. Assam had native tea plants well before the British. The British made tea cultivation a large scale commercial enterprise. From an export-driven industry at its beginning, it has become a part of Indian everyday culture. Indians have made tea their own, with milk, sugar, spices and myriad regional brewing traditions.Today the story of Indian tea is way beyond the familiar cuppa morning chai. From the floral delicacy of Darjeeling’s first flush to the malty strength of Assam’s black teas, and from the aromatic Nilgiris to the complex customs of Kashmiri kahwa, each cup is a unique interaction of geography, climate, cultivation and craft. Even teas grown from the same plant can develop remarkably different flavours depending on when leaves are plucked, how they are withered and rolled and the extent of oxidation they undergo.But to know tea, one must look beyond the cup and into the gardens where it begins. Why does the character of a Darjeeling tea change from 1st flush to 2nd flush? What makes some teas extremely rare and expensive? How do altitude, rainfall, soil and the choices of a tea maker influence aroma, colour and taste? And why can the same leaf make green, black, white and oolong tea?Rudra Chatterjee, Managing Director of Luxmi Tea, gives an insider’s perspective on these less-known sides of India’s tea industry. He turns to India’s tea-making heritage and the intricacies of tea-making to discover 10 distinctive expressions of tea, explaining what makes each variety special, how its character is developed and the traditions that have shaped India’s remarkable tea culture.1. Assam Black Tea: Strong and MaltyAssam’s tropical humidity and the Brahmaputra Valley’s fertile alluvial soils give its teas remarkable body and maltiness. The indigenous Camellia assamica helped establish the region as the world’s greatest tea-growing landscape. A fine orthodox Assam is rounded and complex, while a brisk CTC cup stands up beautifully to milk.2. Darjeeling Black Tea: Cloud in a CupDarjeeling’s spring first flush emerges after the tea bushes have spent winter in dormancy. Growth is slow in the cold, misty Himalayan conditions. Like delicate, slow cooking, first flush requires sensitivity from the tea maker to reveal its subtle bouquet. The cup is often light and floral in character, with greenish leaves interspersed throughout.As days grow longer and warmer, and the monsoons arrive, the second flush develops the celebrated muscatel character, reminiscent of ripe fruit. The same hillside produces dramatically different teas just weeks apart. Drink them without milk, appreciating how changing seasons find expression in the leaf.3. Nilgiri Blue Mountain Tea: The Fragrance of the SouthIn southern India, elevation and cooler weather produce teas valued for their lively aroma, clarity and smoothness. Nilgiri teas become especially fragrant during winter’s colder spells, when slower growth concentrates their character. Their bright, clean flavour makes them excellent both hot and chilled. They remind us that India’s tea story extends far beyond the northeastern mountains.4. White Tea: The Art of Doing LessWhite tea, including Bai Mu Dan, relies on restraint. Tender buds and leaves are withered and dried with minimal manipulation, preserving their delicacy. A good white tea suggests flowers and honey rather than the assertive tannins of black tea.The craftsmanship lies in knowing how little to intervene and in protecting fragile leaves from rough handling. Its subtlety is not for everybody. But on a quiet evening with a book, few cups offer a more contemplative pleasure.5. Silver Tips: When Cultivation Becomes PhilosophyThe silvery hairs covering young buds give Silver Tips its name. Developed at Makaibari in Darjeeling, Silver Tips is a handmade, lightly oxidised oolong produced in tiny quantities, with plucking timed around the full moon. The moonlight plucking reflects a biodynamic tradition, inspired by Rudolf Steiner’s philosophy of treating the farm as an interconnected living organism, attentive to natural rhythms. The resulting cup offers remarkable floral sweetness and delicacy. It is India’s most exclusive and expensive tea.6. Green Tea: A Different Treatment of the Same LeafGreen tea comes from the same plant as black tea. Its leaves are heated early to limit oxidation. Chinese-style pan-firing produces nutty, toasted flavours, while Japanese-style steaming preserves greener, more vegetal notes. Indian tea makers experiment with both approaches. Green tea also provides a canvas for scenting with jasmine flowers, whose fragrance is absorbed by the leaves. The combination illustrates how craftsmanship transforms a familiar leaf. Brew gently; boiling water can scald the tea and overwhelm its finer notes with bitterness.7. Oolong Tea: Between Two WorldsPartially oxidised oolong occupies a spectrum between green and black tea. Some examples are light and floral; others develop fruit, wood or toasted notes through oxidation and roasting. The tea maker’s judgement determines how far these transformations proceed. Repeated infusions reveal different dimensions of the same leaves.8. CTC Black Tea: How India Made Chai Its OwnThere is a delightful irony in India’s national drink. In the early twentieth century, British-backed campaigns promoted tea consumption through railway stalls, demonstrations and advertising. Brooke Bond Kora Dust advertisements became part of this culture. But Indians did not simply adopt the British cup. Households and street vendors transformed strong tea with milk, sugar, ginger, cardamom and other spices into something unmistakably Indian. Later, CTC (crush, tear and curl) processing made brisk, inexpensive tea widely available. Masala chai became a democratic ritual, crossing class, region and language.9. Kashmiri Kahwa: Tea as HospitalityKashmiri kahwa places tea within an older culture of hospitality. Green tea is infused with cardamom, cinnamon and sometimes saffron, then served with almonds. The result is less about the strength of the leaf than the harmony of fragrance, warmth and ceremony. In Kashmir, sharing kahwa is as meaningful as the drink itself. Tea traditions are shaped not only by plantations but by kitchens, gatherings and generations of hospitality.10. Chamomile Infusion: Beyond the Tea PlantChamomile is not technically tea: it comes from flowers rather than Camellia sinensis and is naturally caffeine-free. Yet its growing presence alongside tea reflects interest in botanical infusions and wellbeing. India has its own rich botanical traditions, including tulsi, ashwagandha and moringa, long associated with Ayurveda. These ingredients offer opportunities for new infusions and blends, connecting contemporary tastes with centuries of indigenous knowledge.A Leaf, Many LivesFrom Darjeeling’s misty hillsides to a bustling railway chai stall, India’s teas tell a story of adaptation. The plantation was shaped by empire, but the drink became a language of Indian hospitality, ingenuity and taste. A memorable cup is never simply the leaf. It is the meeting of landscape, craftsmanship and culture that celebrates the remarkable ability of a modest plant to become part of everyday life.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
